chunks: RTL reuse and why it matters. The question: How is RTL reused? Why is this important?
RTL reuse (RTL is the code that describes digital hardware) means writing a hardware block once, carefully, so it can be dropped into many designs without being rewritten.
It matters because designing and testing a block is slow and costly, and testing is usually the bigger cost.
A block that has already been tested, or has already worked in real chips, is much safer than a fresh one. Reuse is not free, though. A flexible block takes more work up front.
Think of a recipe that you scale by servings. The servings number is a setting, so one recipe serves two people or twenty.
Photocopying the recipe and editing each copy by hand is the bad alternative. When you find a mistake, you fix one copy and forget the others.
Parameters are the servings setting in hardware. The recipe picture misses one thing: every extra setting multiplies the combinations you must test.
With these assumed numbers the reusable block overtakes rewriting at about 1. 6 uses, so from the second use on it wins. At 8 uses it is 16 weeks against 48.
The point of the model is the shape (a high fixed cost and a low marginal cost), not the exact numbers; real figures depend on the block.
Parameter: a setting chosen when a block is placed, such as bus width or buffer size. IP block: a reusable design block, built in-house or licensed.
Soft IP: reusable RTL source that you can build for your own chip. Hard IP is a fixed chip layout for one factory process.
Configuration space: all combinations of settings a block supports. Each one needs testing. Testbench: the code that checks a block. It should travel with the block.
Take illustrative numbers. Writing and testing a single-use block takes 6 weeks. Making it reusable takes 9 weeks, and each later use takes 1 week to integrate.
Over 5 projects, rewriting costs 6 times 5 equals 30 weeks. Reuse costs 9 plus 4 times 1 equals 13 weeks, saving 17. The cost of flexibility shows up too.
With 10 independent on/off options, a block has 2 to the 10 equals 1024 combinations, far too many to test, so you limit the options. That is the whole idea.
"RTL reuse is writing a block once, with parameters and clean interfaces, so it can drop into many designs.
Tools are parameters, generate statements, packages, interfaces, and standard bus protocols.
It matters because it saves schedule and, more importantly, verification effort, and a block already proven in silicon is lower risk.
The cost is that a reusable block needs documentation, a limited and well-tested configuration space, and a testbench that travels with it, instead of copy-paste edits that drift apart."
